courseTitle: How IT Teams Work: Agile, Waterfall, Scrum, Kanban & Software Releases

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a project you've personally been part of (a work task, a school project, even planning an event). Write one paragraph describing it as a Waterfall project (fixed phases, signed off up front) and a second paragraph describing the same project run as Agile (short cycles, adapting as you learn). Note specifically where a late-discovered requirement would have been expensive under Waterfall but cheap under Agile.
slots.deliverable: A short written comparison (2 paragraphs) of one real project modeled both ways, naming the specific point where a late change would cost more under Waterfall.

slots.practicalActivity: Invent a small feature request (e.g. 'add a dark mode toggle to an app'). Write 3 real user stories for it in the 'As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]' format, each with 2 concrete acceptance criteria. Then write a one-paragraph sprint plan: what would go into a 2-week sprint, and what would be held back for later.
slots.deliverable: 3 written user stories with acceptance criteria, plus a short sprint-scoping paragraph for the same feature.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a real Kanban board for the same feature from the previous slot, either in a free tool (Trello, GitHub Projects, Notion) or on paper/spreadsheet, with Backlog, To Do, In Progress, Review, and Done columns. Place your 3 user stories plus 2 additional small tasks you invent (e.g. 'write test cases', 'update settings docs') into the board, then move at least one card all the way from Backlog to Done to prove the flow works.
slots.deliverable: A Kanban board (tool screenshot, exported image, or photo of a physical board) with at least 5 cards and one card moved end-to-end through all 5 columns.

slots.practicalActivity: Take the dark-mode feature and write, environment by environment, exactly what happens to it: what a developer does in Dev, what a QA tester checks before promoting it, what the business owner does during UAT, and what 'live' means once it reaches Production. For each environment, name one thing that could go wrong there specifically (not in a different environment).
slots.deliverable: A 4-part written walkthrough (Dev, QA, UAT, Production) of one feature's journey, each part naming a realistic failure specific to that environment.

slots.practicalActivity: Install Git if it isn't already on your machine, create a scratch folder, run git init, create a file, and run git add and git commit with a real descriptive message (not 'update'). Make a second commit after another small change, then run git log to see both commits, and git status in between to see the before/after state.
slots.deliverable: A terminal transcript or screenshot showing git init, two real commits with descriptive messages, and the resulting git log output.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a real release note for the dark-mode feature in the style the lesson demonstrates: what was added, any known limitation, and anything the audience needs to know — in 2-3 specific sentences, not a vague 'various improvements'. Then sketch (as a short bullet list) the CI/CD pipeline that would carry this change from a developer's commit to production, naming which step is Continuous Integration, which is Delivery, and which (if any) is Deployment.
slots.deliverable: One specific, non-vague release note, plus a labeled 3-step pipeline sketch (CI / Delivery / Deployment) for the same change.

slots.practicalActivity: Work through the full Castlebridge Retail capstone from the lesson: turn the sales director's one-paragraph request into real user stories with acceptance criteria, build a Kanban board for it, write a short QA test plan (including the zero-sales edge case), write a one-paragraph UAT sign-off in the sales director's voice, write specific release notes, and write up how you'd investigate and communicate about the 'numbers show zero' production incident two days after launch.
slots.deliverable: A complete capstone packet: user stories with acceptance criteria, a Kanban board, a QA test plan with one named edge case, a UAT sign-off paragraph, release notes, and a production-incident response write-up.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can read and actively participate in how a real IT team plans, builds, tests, and ships work — fluent in Agile/Scrum/Kanban vocabulary, the Dev/QA/UAT/Production chain, basic Git, and CI/CD — and has personally simulated one full business request through to a handled production incident.
